analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to disclose who funded studies they submit to influence federal rules.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a hearing, markup, or vote — it was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee the day it was introduced and the Congress ended five months later.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted how corporations quietly shape federal regulations. When companies submit scientific or economic studies to influence a rule, they would have to disclose who funded the study, whether the company reviewed or edited it, and any financial ties between the researchers and parties affected by the rule. Agencies would have to post those studies and flag industry-funded ones publicly, could ignore undisclosed submissions, and could fine publicly traded companies $250,000 or more for knowingly submitting false information.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, patients, and communities affected by federal health, safety, environmental, and financial rules would gain visibility into whose money is behind the research used to shape those rules. The bill also creates an Office of the Public Advocate to help ordinary people participate in rulemaking, requires agencies to answer petitions with 100,000+ signatures, caps White House review of major rules at 60 days so protective rules cannot sit stalled, requires public explanation when agencies quietly withdraw or change rules, and restores courts' practice of deferring to agencies' reasonable readings of ambiguous laws.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People affected by federal health and safety rules

how_it_helps.text: Requires anyone submitting a study in a rulemaking to disclose the funding amount, the funder's identity, whether anyone was allowed to review or revise the findings, and any financial relationship between the researchers and parties affected by the rule.

Requires agencies to make submitted studies publicly available on their websites and dockets, and to publicly flag conflicts where 10% or more of a study's funding comes from an entity the agency regulates or where that entity exercises editorial control over the research.

Lets agencies disregard submissions that violate the disclosure rules, and imposes civil penalties on publicly traded companies starting at $250,000 for a first knowing false statement and $1,000,000 for each repeat violation.

Requires agencies to disclose in the public docket what changed between their draft rules and the versions published after White House (OIRA) review, and to explain in detail why any rule was withdrawn and whether outside officials requested it — exposing backroom edits.

Caps White House review of major rules at 60 days (extendable once, with written justification), after which the agency can publish the rule without further OIRA sign-off, so the review process cannot be used to quietly kill protective rules.

Restricts 'negotiated rulemaking' — committees that draft rules by consensus — to Federal, State, local, and Tribal governments, removing industry's formal seat at that table and repealing negotiated-rulemaking requirements across education, health, housing, and other laws.

Creates an Office of the Public Advocate inside the budget office to help ordinary people and underrepresented communities participate in rulemaking, in plain language and multiple languages, and to produce social-equity assessments of proposed rules.

Restores judicial deference to agencies' reasonable interpretations of ambiguous statutes (a response to the Supreme Court's 2024 Loper Bright decision), and requires agencies to respond in writing within 60 days to petitions signed by more than 100,000 people.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and the consulting firms they hire to produce regulatory research would bear the direct costs: compiling and disclosing funding and financial-relationship details, losing the ability to shape rules through undisclosed or privately edited studies, and — for publicly traded companies — potential fines of $250,000 to $1,000,000 or more for false filings. Industry also loses its formal role in negotiated rulemaking and its ability to use White House review as a quiet veto. Federal agencies would take on new disclosure, publication, and public-participation duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations that fund studies to shape federal rules

drawbacks.text: The bill would reverse the Supreme Court's June 2024 Loper Bright ruling by writing judicial deference to agency interpretations back into federal law — its most legally contested provision, which critics across the spectrum said hands too much power to unelected officials and would draw immediate constitutional challenges.

It directs agencies to prioritize rules' public benefits and forbids courts from requiring agencies to justify actions against a cost-benefit standard, which business groups argue could produce regulations whose costs exceed their benefits, with those costs passed on to consumers through higher prices.

The penalties for false submissions apply only to companies that file SEC annual reports — privately held companies, trade associations, and industry-funded advocacy groups would face disclosure requirements but no fines, leaving an enforcement gap.

The 60-day limit on White House review could rush sign-off on complex or novel rules, and abolishing private-party participation in negotiated rulemaking eliminates a process that sometimes produced consensus rules without litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — disclosure of who funded and edited the research used to shape federal rules — addresses a real imbalance at modest cost: today, industry-funded and industry-edited studies can dominate a regulatory docket with no one the wiser, while the public has no way to check them. The compliance burden on companies is real but light, and the penalty gap for privately held firms is a genuine design flaw. The bill's more ambitious structural provisions — reinstating Chevron-style deference, prioritizing benefits over cost-benefit math, and ending negotiated rulemaking — are the parts most likely to draw litigation and fierce opposition, and honest supporters would acknowledge they go well beyond the transparency fix. On balance, the transparency provisions would clearly help ordinary people; the broader reworking of the regulatory state is more contested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Stop Corporate Capture Act on July 23, 2024, joined by ten cosponsors — nine Democrats and one Independent.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, the standard first step.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed — the action history shows nothing after the referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee with no recorded vote of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate interests that fund studies and file comments to shape federal rules are better off, because the disclosure requirements, public conflict flagging, and $250,000+ fines never took effect. The status quo — in which industry-funded research can enter the rulemaking record without its funding disclosed — continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that fund studies to shape rules

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Corporate Capture Act on July 23, 2024, based on her long-running oversight of industry influence in rulemaking.

for.name: Sens. Sanders, Blumenthal, Merkley, Hirono, Lujan, Van Hollen, Markey, Wyden, Booker, and Welch
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors — all Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican joined.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (Chair Sen. Gary Peters)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or committee vote; the bill's only action was the referral itself and it died there.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with the bill stalled in committee, no floor vote was ever scheduled in the Democratic-controlled Senate.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the House-passed version of this bill in a prior Congress, arguing the disclosure mandates, penalties, and limits on industry input would burden companies and invite litigation.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Democrats or Independent Bernie Sanders, no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted — so the bill's fate was decided within one party rather than by an explicit partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill would force companies and trade groups to disclose who funded the studies they submit in rulemaking, whether they edited the findings, and their financial ties to affected parties — and would let agencies throw out undisclosed submissions entirely. That ends the practice of shaping health, safety, and financial rules through research whose funding is never revealed.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (drug, chemical, energy, and financial firms)
industries.note: These companies would face public flagging of studies where they supply 10%+ of funding or exercise editorial control, fines for false filings, loss of their formal seat in negotiated rulemaking, and a 60-day cap on White House review that limits their ability to quietly stall or reshape protective rules.

industries.industry: Economic and scientific consulting firms serving regulated clients
industries.note: The disclosure regime would expose the funding behind consultants' regulatory studies and force researchers to reveal financial relationships with affected parties, discouraging some industry work; demand for regulatory analysis would continue, but only in the open.
